Imperfect Data

Session 9

2026-11-03

The study you run is not the study you planned

  • Your PAP describes the study you planned.
  • The study that runs departs from it:
    • some participants won’t use the tool
    • some API calls time out
    • some judge outputs fail to parse.
  • Each departure changes what the data can tell you.
  • Your job after registration:
    • measure every departure
    • analyze the study you actually ran
    • report the gap against the plan.

Analyses you planned are confirmatory.

Analyses you chose after seeing the data are exploratory.

Planned design, realized design

  • The PAP declares a design: Model, Inquiry, Data strategy, Answer strategy.
  • Each part of the data strategy is carried out imperfectly:
    • Sampling: who or what actually enters the study.
    • Assignment: who actually receives each treatment.
    • Measurement: which outcomes are actually recorded.

Planned

  • 200 participants, 100 offered the tutor.
  • Everyone offered the tutor uses it.
  • Every quiz is scored.

Realized

  • 194 start; 61 of the 97 offered open the tutor.
  • 23 leave before the quiz, 17 of them in the tutor arm.
  • 4 free-text answers fail to parse.
  • End the study with a realized design to compare with the planned design.
    • Diagnose it like the plan.

Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), Research Design in the Social Sciences, Princeton University Press, ch. 22.

How AI evaluations go wrong

Treatment received differs

  • Participants offered the tool never open it.
  • Control participants use ChatGPT anyway.
  • The agent skips the retrieval tool call.
  • A router falls back to another model.
  • \(\implies\) noncompliance

Outcome goes missing

  • Participants leave before the outcome.
  • Calls time out or hit rate limits.
  • The model refuses.
  • The judge’s output fails to parse.
  • \(\implies\) attrition

The instrument changes

  • A model alias points to a new snapshot mid-study.
  • The provider retires your pinned snapshot.
  • \(\implies\) treatment changes for everyone at once
  • GPT-4, March to June 2023. Prime identification fell from 84% to 51%. Directly executable code fell from 52% to 10%, mostly from added markdown fences.

Chen, Zaharia & Zou (2024), How Is ChatGPT’s Behavior Changing over Time?, Harvard Data Science Review 6(2).

Noncompliance

Assigned treatment versus received treatment

  • Running example: 200 participants study for a 0–100 quiz. A random 100 are offered an AI tutor.
  • \(Z_i=1\) if participant \(i\) is assigned the tutor.
  • \(D_i(z)\): whether \(i\) receives it under assignment \(z\). Observed: \(D_i=D_i(Z_i)\), here “opened the tutor at least once”.
  • \(Y_i(z)\): \(i\)’s quiz score under assignment \(z\).
  • Randomization controls \(Z_i\). Participants choose \(D_i\).
  • Model-only studies have the same gap. The retrieval Bundle’s agent decides whether to call the retrieval tool.
    • \(D_i=1\) only if retrieval actually ran on question \(i\).
  • Motivated participants open the tutor (\(D_i=1\)) and would score higher without it.
  • Comparing takers (\(D_i=1\)) to non-takers (\(D_i=0\)) compares different kinds of people.

Take-up in AI-tool field experiments

  • Cui et al.: GitHub Copilot access randomized among developers at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm.
  • Microsoft, 1,746 developers:
    • 8.5% of the treated group signed up in the first two weeks.
    • Two reminder emails raised take-up to 42.5%.
  • Across the three firms, 30–40% of treated engineers never tried the tool.

  • Gerber & Green: “The subjects who are actually treated are a non-random subset of the original treatment group. This point cannot be emphasized enough.”
  • The developers who adopted early are the ones most eager for the tool.

Cui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng & Salz (2025), The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers, Management Science.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments: Design, Analysis, and Interpretation, Norton, ch. 5, p. 134.

The intent-to-treat effect survives

  • The intent-to-treat (ITT) effect is the effect of being assigned:

\[\mathrm{ITT}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\big[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\big],\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}=\bar Y_{Z=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0}.\]

  • Random assignment makes \(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}\) unbiased, whatever participants do afterwards.
    • Its standard error is lecture 06’s difference-in-means SE.
  • Take-up has its own ITT: \(\mathrm{ITT}_D=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\big[D_i(1)-D_i(0)\big]\).
    • Estimated by \(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}_D=\bar D_{Z=1}-\bar D_{Z=0}\).
  • The ITT answers a deployment question: what happens when you offer the tool?
    • Deployment also offers. Users decide whether to use it.
  • Report it first, as the primary analysis.

One-sided noncompliance and the complier effect

  • One-sided: only the treatment arm can deviate. \(D_i(0)=0\) for everyone.
  • Compliers take the tutor when offered: \(D_i(1)=1\). Never-takers do not: \(D_i(1)=0\).
  • Assignment cannot change a never-taker’s score, so the ITT is the compliers’ effect, diluted:

\[\mathrm{ITT}=\mathrm{ITT}_D\cdot\mathrm{CACE}+(1-\mathrm{ITT}_D)\cdot 0.\]

  • So the complier average causal effect is the ITT scaled up by take-up:

\[\mathrm{CACE}=\operatorname{E}\big[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid D_i(1)=1\big]=\frac{\mathrm{ITT}}{\mathrm{ITT}_D}.\]

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments: Design, Analysis, and Interpretation, Norton, ch. 5, Theorem 5.1.

Estimating the complier effect

\[\widehat{\mathrm{CACE}}=\frac{\bar Y_{Z=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0}}{\bar D_{Z=1}-\bar D_{Z=0}},\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\big(\widehat{\mathrm{CACE}}\big)\approx\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\big(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}\big)}{\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}_D}.\]

  • This is instrumental variables with \(Z\) as the instrument. Two-stage least squares gives the same estimate: iv_robust(Y ~ D | Z, data).
  • Gerber & Green, New Haven 1998: 1,445 people assigned a get-out-the-vote canvass, 5,645 controls.
    • Turnout 41.4% against 37.5%: \(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}=3.8\) points.
    • Canvassers reached 395 of the 1,445: \(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}_D=0.27\).
    • \(\widehat{\mathrm{CACE}}=3.84/0.273=14.1\) points, 95% CI 3.8 to 24.3.
  • Cui et al.: Copilot adoption raised completed pull requests by 26% (SE 10%).

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 5, Table 5.2.

Cui et al. (2025), Management Science.

Simulation: four ways to analyze one study

  • Simulation: 60% of participants would open the tutor if offered. The tutor adds 6 points for them. Motivated participants open it more and score higher anyway.
  • As treated compares everyone who opened the tutor with everyone who did not. Per protocol drops treated participants who never opened it.
  • Both compare motivated takers with a less motivated group. Both overstate the 6-point effect.
    • In New Haven, the canvassed against controls gives 16.9 points, against the CACE of 14.1.

What the complier effect assumes

  • The ITT needs random assignment and non-interference. The CACE adds two assumptions.
  • Excludability: assignment matters only through receipt, \(Y_i(z,d)=Y_i(d)\).
    • Fails if participants told they have a tutor study less, whether or not they open it.
    • Fails if the retrieval Bundle’s system prompt mentions course materials even when retrieval never runs.
  • A direct effect \(\delta\) on never-takers biases the ratio by \(\delta\,(1-\mathrm{ITT}_D)/\mathrm{ITT}_D\). At 20% take-up that is \(4\delta\).
  • Non-interference: \(i\)’s outcome depends only on \(i\)’s own assignment.
    • Fails if participants share tutor answers in a course group chat.
    • Fails if both arms share one rate limit, so treatment calls slow down control calls.
  • One-sidedness: the control arm has no access. Control participants using another chatbot make it two-sided.

Two-sided noncompliance

Type \(D_i(0)\) \(D_i(1)\)
Never-taker 0 0
Complier 0 1
Always-taker 1 1
Defier 1 0
  • Always-takers use an AI tool whatever they are assigned, like controls who use ChatGPT anyway.
  • Defiers use one only when told not to.
  • Monotonicity: \(D_i(1)\ge D_i(0)\) for every \(i\). There are no defiers.
  • Under monotonicity and excludability the same ratio identifies the CACE:

\[\mathrm{CACE}=\frac{\mathrm{ITT}}{\mathrm{ITT}_D},\qquad \mathrm{ITT}_D=\Pr(\text{complier}).\]

  • Gerber & Green, NYC mayoral debate: viewing encouraged at random. 20.5% compliers, 16.2% always-takers, 63.4% never-takers. \(\widehat{\mathrm{CACE}}=0.057/0.205=0.28\).

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 6, Tables 6.2–6.3.

Who are the compliers?

  • The CACE is the effect for compliers only. Nobody is labeled a complier in the data.
    • A treated taker might be a complier or an always-taker.
  • Their share is identified: \(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}_D\).
  • Under one-sided noncompliance, the treated takers are the compliers. Their pretreatment covariates are visible.
  • Simulation, one study: 52% of those offered open the tutor. Their mean prior grade is +0.45 SD, against +0.07 for everyone.
  • The CACE describes motivated, higher-achieving students.
  • Ask which population your decision concerns.
    • A tool everyone will be required to use: the CACE speaks only for compliers.
    • A tool users can choose: the ITT at deployment’s take-up rate.

Low take-up costs power

  • \(N=200\), 6 points for compliers.
  • \(\mathrm{ITT}=\mathrm{ITT}_D\cdot\mathrm{CACE}\), so the sample needed grows as \(1/\mathrm{ITT}_D^{2}\).
    • Planned take-up 90%, realized 40%: about \((0.9/0.4)^2\approx5\) times the sample.
  • Gerber & Green: take-up falling from 100% to 10% needs 100 times the sample.
  • Raising take-up is usually cheaper than recruiting. Default the tool on, onboard participants, send reminders.
    • Cui et al.: two reminder emails took Copilot take-up from 8.5% to 42.5%.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 5, p. 161.

Summary: noncompliance

  • Analyze as assigned first: \(\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}=\bar Y_{Z=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0}\) is unbiased whatever participants do.
  • \(\widehat{\mathrm{CACE}}=\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}/\widehat{\mathrm{ITT}}_D\) is the effect for compliers. It assumes excludability, non-interference, and monotonicity.
  • As-treated and per-protocol comparisons select on a post-assignment choice. In the simulation they overstate the effect.
  • Report the take-up rate and the compliers’ covariate profile next to the CACE.
  • Power falls with take-up squared. Design for take-up.

Attrition

Missing outcomes break the comparison

  • \(R_i(z)=1\) if unit \(i\)’s outcome is recorded under assignment \(z\).
  • Dropping missing rows gives the complete-case estimator:

\[\hat\Delta_{\text{cc}}=\bar Y_{Z=1,R=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0,R=1}.\]

  • Randomization balanced the arms before anyone went missing.
  • When missingness differs by arm, the units that remain can differ in ways that also drive the outcome.
  • RAND Health Insurance Experiment: families randomized to plans ranging from free care to paying most costs themselves.
    • 8% refused to enroll in the free plan, 25% in the plan with the most cost sharing. Their outcomes are missing.
    • Families expecting large medical bills had the most reason to refuse cost sharing. The cost-sharing arms that remain look healthier.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 7, pp. 212–214.

Aron-Dine, Einav & Finkelstein (2013), The RAND Health Insurance Experiment, Three Decades Later, Journal of Economic Perspectives 27(1).

Running example: refusals in a labelling task

  • Model-only study: an LLM labels 1,000 posts as hateful or not. Expert gold labels exist for all of them.
  • A random 500 get a codebook prompt that asks the model to quote the hateful phrase. The rest get a one-line instruction.
  • \(Y_i=100\) if the model’s label matches gold, 0 if not.
  • The model refuses 3% of posts at random under either prompt.
  • Under the codebook it also refuses to quote the most explicit posts.
  • Explicit posts are the easiest to label. \(\hat\Delta_{\text{cc}}\) compares harder codebook posts with all the others.
  • Prompts move refusal rates a lot. Röttger et al.: Llama-2-70b-chat refused 38% of 250 safe prompts with its default system prompt, 14% without.

Röttger et al. (2024), XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models, NAACL.

When missingness is harmless

  • Missing independent of potential outcomes (MIPO):

\[Y_i(z)\perp R_i(z).\]

  • Under MIPO, the recorded units in each arm are a random subsample. \(\hat\Delta_{\text{cc}}\) is unbiased.
  • MIPO given covariates: \(Y_i(z)\perp R_i(z)\mid X_i\). Reweight each recorded unit by its arm’s response rate \(\hat q_z(X_i)\) at its covariate value:

\[\hat\mu_z=\frac{\sum_{i:Z_i=z}R_iY_i/\hat q_z(X_i)}{\sum_{i:Z_i=z}R_i/\hat q_z(X_i)}.\]

  • Both are claims about outcomes you did not see. Neither can be tested.
  • In the refusal example, MIPO fails: refusals (\(R_i=0\)) concentrate on explicit posts, which have high \(Y_i\).

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 7.

Diagnosing attrition

  • Equal attrition rates are weak reassurance. Run two checks:
    1. Attrition by arm: regress \(R_i\) on \(Z_i\). A difference means treatment changes who is missing.
    2. Who is missing: regress \(R_i\) on \(Z_i\), \(X_i\), and \(Z_iX_i\). An interaction means treatment changes which units go missing.
      • \(X_i\): a toxicity score from an off-the-shelf classifier, computed before assignment.
One simulated study
Arm Posts Refused Toxicity, labelled Toxicity, refused
Codebook 500 82 -0.21 0.72
One-line instruction 500 10 0.04 0.01
  • The codebook’s labelled share is 14 points lower, \(p<0.001\). Interaction with toxicity: \(p<0.001\).

Bounding the effect

  • Extreme-value bounds: fill every missing outcome with the scale’s minimum or maximum. With \(q_z\) the share recorded in arm \(z\):

\[\Delta^{\pm}=\big[q_1\bar Y_{1}^{R=1}+(1-q_1)\,y^{\pm}\big]-\big[q_0\bar Y_{0}^{R=1}+(1-q_0)\,y^{\mp}\big].\]

  • Here \(y^{+}=100\) (correct) and \(y^{-}=0\) (wrong). The width is \((2-q_0-q_1)\times100\) points, whatever the data say.
  • Trimming bounds (Lee): assume monotonicity: the codebook can only cause a refusal, \(R_i(1)\le R_i(0)\).
    • The arm with fewer refusals holds extra units. Trim the share \(p=(q_0-q_1)/q_0\) from its top or its bottom:

\[\Delta^{\text{lower}}=\bar Y_{1}^{R=1}-\bar Y_{0}^{R=1,\,\text{top }1-p},\qquad \Delta^{\text{upper}}=\bar Y_{1}^{R=1}-\bar Y_{0}^{R=1,\,\text{bottom }1-p}.\]

  • These bound the effect on always-labelled posts, labelled under either prompt.

Lee (2009), Training, Wages, and Sample Selection: Estimating Sharp Bounds on Treatment Effects, Review of Economic Studies 76(3).

Simulation: estimates under differential refusals

  • Studies of 5,000 posts. The codebook raises accuracy by 6.4 points. It is refused on 16% of posts, against 3% without it.
  • Thin bars span the middle 95% of studies. Complete case: 2.8 on average. Its interval covers 28% of the time.
  • Thick bars are the bounds averaged over studies: trimming [-6.7, 8.2], extreme-value [-8.7, 9.9].
    • With a 0/1 outcome, trimming removes only correct labels or only wrong ones. It buys little.

Bounds on real data

  • Gerber & Green, Colombian school vouchers (PACES): 3,542 lottery applicants, 2,073 winners.
    • Test scores exist only for students who registered for the national exam.
    • 37.6% of winners registered, against 30.2% of losers.
  • Complete case: 47.6 against 46.9, a difference of 0.7 points.
  • Extreme-value bounds on the 0–100 scale: [−66.1, 66.1].
  • Trimming bounds: trim 19.6% of the winners’ scores. [−0.8, 2.7].
  • A continuous score lets trimming work. Accuracy on a 0/1 scale does not.
  • Bounds are estimates too. Their endpoints have sampling error.
    • An interval for the bounds widens them further (Imbens & Manski 2004).

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 7, pp. 230–236.

Imbens & Manski (2004), Confidence Intervals for Partially Identified Parameters, Econometrica 72(6).

Spending effort on the missing

  • Double sampling: after the main collection, draw a random subsample of the units with missing outcomes. Spend heavily to measure them.
  • The subsample stands in for all missing units in its arm:

\[\hat\mu_z=q_z\,\bar Y_z^{R=1}+(1-q_z)\,\bar Y_z^{\text{follow-up}}.\]

  • If some follow-ups also fail, bound only those.
  • Gerber & Green simulation: true effect 0.10, complete case 0.001, with a random follow-up 0.085.
  • In an AI evaluation, follow-up is often cheap. For a random sample:
    • rerun timed-out calls with a longer timeout
    • hand-score unparseable judge outputs
    • pay dropouts a bonus to finish the outcome survey.
  • The sample must be random. Chasing the easiest cases first breaks it.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 7.6, Table 7.6.

Refusals: missing data or an outcome?

  • A moderation system classifies every post with the codebook prompt. The model refuses some posts, mostly the most explicit ones.

Measuring the classifier: missing data

  • How accurate are the model’s classifications?
  • A refusal produces no classification. The post stays unlabelled.
  • Treat it as missing. Bound the codebook’s effect on accuracy.

Measuring the system: an outcome

  • How accurate are the system’s decisions?
  • A refusal still ends in a decision, explicit or by default. Here the post stays up.
  • Score that decision. A hateful post left up is an error.
  • What a refusal means depends on the system around the model and the question you ask of it.
  • Simply dropping missing values will not likely be the ideal solution.

Summary: attrition

  • Dropping missing rows is unbiased only under MIPO, \(Y_i(z)\perp R_i(z)\). MIPO cannot be tested.
  • Diagnose attrition by arm, and by pretreatment covariates within arm.
  • Bounds drop the assumption. Extreme-value bounds are always valid and often wide. Trimming bounds assume monotonicity, and won’t help much with 0/1 outcomes.
  • A random follow-up sample of the missing may help.
  • What a refusal means depends on the system and the question.

Pivoting

Continue or change the design

  • Re-diagnose the design at your pilot’s take-up, refusal, and attrition rates, and at its outcome distributions.
  • Continue when the realized design still answers the question.
  • Change the design when it does not.
  • Example: the primary outcome barely varies.
    • The model answers 98% of items correctly under both prompts. It has almost no room to move.
  • The primary hypothesis may move to an outcome that varies. Every registered outcome is still reported.
Original plan Deviation Reason
Primary: accuracy on all items Primary: accuracy on hard items Ceiling effects

Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), Research Design in the Social Sciences, ch. 22.1.

Reporting the realized design

  • Lecture 07’s reconciliation tables list each departure from the plan. Report the realized design next to them:
    • Data strategy: take-up, attrition, and refusals by arm. Every model id the provider reported.
    • Inquiry: the estimand behind each number. ITT or CACE; accuracy on labelled posts or the pipeline’s decisions.
    • Answer strategy: the registered estimate first. Then the CACE and the bounds, labeled as such.
  • Re-diagnose at the realized rates: power, bias, and coverage.
  • A reader can then judge how much to trust the answer.

Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), Research Design in the Social Sciences, ch. 22.4.

Before session 10

For next week

  • Session 10 is a workshop. Bring some initial data.

What is arriving

  • take-up, refusals, and attrition by arm
  • the outcome’s distribution in each arm
  • API errors, timeouts, and unparseable judge output
  • the model ids the API reports

How it differs from the plan

  • rates against those in your diagnosis
  • outcomes stuck at a ceiling or floor
  • failures your pipeline does not handle yet
  • units that look different from the ones you expected
  • Re-diagnose plugging in what you now know about your data. Come with a first call: continue, or change the design and record the deviation.

Next week’s readings

  • Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), ch. 22 “Realization”: every team. Pivoting, the populated PAP, reconciliation, and writing up the design you ran.
  • Gerber & Green (2012), as useful for your study:
    • ch. 5, one-sided noncompliance: treated units can decline the treatment. Participants never open the tool; the agent skips the tool call.
    • ch. 6, two-sided noncompliance: control units can get it too. Control participants use ChatGPT; a router sends control calls to the treatment model.
    • ch. 7, attrition: outcomes go missing. Dropouts, refusals in a labelling task, timeouts, unparseable judge output.
  • Reflection memos on these readings: post by 9 November, 24 hours before session 10.
